nameStory: The 'minutus' in this spider's scientific name comes from the Latin word meaning 'small' or 'minute,' highlighting just how tiny this running crab spider really is. Like other running crab spiders, it gets its common name from its crab-like appearance and its habit of running sideways and backwards with surprising speed, rather than building webs to catch prey.
description: The Minute Running Crab Spider is one of the tiniest members of the running crab spider family found in New England. These diminutive hunters have the characteristic flattened, crab-like body shape with legs that extend sideways from their body. They're active predators that chase down small prey rather than spinning webs, using their speed and agility to catch insects much like a tiny eight-legged cheetah. Due to their small size, they're easily overlooked unless you're looking very carefully.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Exceptionally small even for crab spiders, with a body that feels almost weightless if it walks across your hand and legs that span less than the width of your pinky nail

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly flattened and crab-like with a relatively wide abdomen that appears pressed down, giving it a pancake-like profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with quick, jerky motions and can run sideways or backwards with startling speed when disturbed, often freezing completely when it thinks it's been spotted

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build capture webs but may leave tiny silk draglines that feel like the finest thread when accidentally brushed against

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight small eyes arranged in two rows, with the front row slightly curved and eyes that appear as tiny black dots even under magnification

habitat: Found on low vegetation, tree bark, and among leaf litter in forests and woodland edges throughout New England. They prefer areas with abundant small prey insects and seem to favor spots with dappled sunlight where they can easily hide against textured surfaces. Look for them hunting on shrubs, ferns, and the lower branches of deciduous trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting season on emerging vegetation. This is when they're most likely to be spotted as they search for mates and establish territories.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and easiest to find actively hunting during warm days. Egg sacs may be found attached to vegetation during late summer.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, though they become less conspicuous as they prepare for winter. Young spiders may be found dispersing to new territories.
seasonality.winter: Overwinter in protected locations under bark, in leaf litter, or other sheltered spots, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being so small they could comfortably sit on the head of a pin, Minute Running Crab Spiders are capable of taking down prey insects that are significantly larger than themselves, sometimes wrestling with gnats and small flies that outweigh them!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other tiny running crab spiders in the same genus, but the exceptionally small size of minutus helps distinguish it from most relatives. Remember: if you're questioning whether a running crab spider is unusually tiny, it might just be this species.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England according to current data, this species may be either genuinely rare in the region or simply so small and inconspicuous that it's severely under-reported by citizen scientists and researchers alike.
compareHints: The Minute Running Crab Spider is significantly smaller than its relatives like the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, which are much more commonly encountered. While other Philodromus species may have distinctive coloration or markings, minutus is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally small size. Unlike the more robust Turf Running Spider, minutus appears almost delicate in build.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the White-striped Running Crab Spider which has obvious white stripes, the metallic crab spider males are uniformly shiny without stripes.

The white-striped running crab spider is distinguished from its relatives by those prominent longitudinal white stripes - most other Philodromus species in New England have more subtle markings or different color patterns.

The Turf Running Spider differs from its Philodromus relatives primarily in habitat preference - while the Metallic Crab Spider tends toward trees and the White-striped Running Crab Spider prefers taller shrubs, the Turf Running Spider sticks to low vegetation and ground cover.

Compared to other Philodromus species in New England, the Resplendent Running Crab Spider stands out for its particularly brilliant metallic appearance - more lustrous than the Metallic Crab Spider and lacking the white stripes of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.

Among its Philodromus relatives in New England, the male's distinctive shiny black coloration with white edges makes it relatively easy to distinguish from the more uniformly colored Metallic Crab Spider or the striped patterns of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.
Philodromus exilis is notably more slender than the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, lacking the metallic sheen or distinct striping of those relatives.
